title: Allow multiple elements with the same nearest ancestor `autofocus` scoping root element to have `autofocus`
body:
### What is the issue with the HTML Standard?

According to [6.6.7 The `autofocus` attribute](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#the-autofocus-attribute),

> There must not be two elements with the same [nearest ancestor autofocus scoping root element](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#nearest-ancestor-autofocus-scoping-root-element) that both have the [autofocus](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/interaction.html#attr-fe-autofocus) attribute specified.

My thinking is that this restriction could, and maybe should, be relaxed for the following reasons:

1. The HTML spec's algorithm (and current browsers) allows for multiple elements with `autofocus`
2. Using `autofocus` liberally can make the authoring process simpler

On point 2, I'm thinking of a situation where you have composed components in a framework like React or Svelte. Consider an example of a menu popover:

```jsx
<PopoverMenu>
  <PopoverMenuTrigger>Open Menu</PopoverMenuTrigger>

  <PopoverMenuItems>
    <PopoverMenuItem>Item 1</PopoverMenuItem>
    <PopoverMenuItem>Item 2</PopoverMenuItem>
    <PopoverMenuItem>Item 3</PopoverMenuItem>
  <PopoverMenuItems>
</PopoverMenu>
```

In this scenario, it is natural to want to bake the `autofocus` behaviour into `PopoverMenuItem` logic. Doing so would mean a consumer of this component would be covered if they didn't consider the accessibility aspects. However, only applying `autofocus` to the first item adds unnecessary complexity in these frameworks because they typically have one-way data flow, meaning it's unnatural for `<PopoverMenuItem>` to feed back up the tree that it has consumed the `autofocus` flag for a future `<PopoverMenuItem>` to omit the attribute. Additionally, the first item may also not necessarily be the one that automatically receives focus—for instance, if it is not focusable (e.g. it is in a disabled state)—, so even implementing all the complexity required will require the author to consider the spec's criteria in advance to avoid failures in accessibility.

As mentioned before, the spec's algorithm allows for multiple candidates, and any non-focusable candidate is eliminated. Thus, adding `autofocus` to every element in this scenario **works surprisingly well**, with the rather large downside of **not passing validation**.

In summary, my understanding is that this restriction serves no _functional_ purpose and no harm or compatibility issues would arise from its removal, yet it would ease authoring friction.
